title: Driver-Sourced Dock Queue Index for Funds
one_liner: Pay verified truckers to report what they see at plants, ports and distribution centers, and sell the resulting real-economy index to funds, credit analysts and site-selection teams.
customer: Small and mid-size quant and fundamental hedge funds, equity and credit research shops covering industrials and retail, private-credit lenders to retailers and manufacturers, and commercial real-estate investors. Annual subscriptions of $25k to $150k per sector index.
problem: Alt-data vendors see parking lots from satellites and card swipes from panels, but nobody sees the freight dock. Telematics vendors sell dwell time at a geofence but not what's moving, whether the yard is full, or whether appointments are being cancelled. Tariff shocks in 2025 to 2026 made import front-loading, steel inventory builds and retailer DC slowdowns critical to read weeks earlier. The alt-data market was about $2.8B in 2025 and most institutional funds use several sources, but trucking signals stay coarse.
solution: A watchlist of about 500 facilities mapped to public tickers (steel mills, Amazon and Walmart DCs, Home Depot and Costco DCs, auto plants, ports and rail ramps). Drivers whose ELD or phone geofence confirms they are at the site file a 30-second structured report: queue length, hours waited, outbound commodity, trailers stacked or pulled, yard fullness, appointments cancelled, 'no freight today'. Pay $3 to $8 per accepted report. Aggregate into weekly facility, sector and regional indices. Only publicly observable facts are collected, with no shipper confidential documents and no insider employees. A securities lawyer reviews the collection rules before launch.
why_now: Tariff-driven import and inventory swings make physical-economy signals more valuable than ever. Freight recession conditions mean lots of idle drivers willing to earn side income while waiting. Geofence verification, instant payouts and modern OCR/LLM structuring make a human-observation network cheap to run. Fund appetite for differentiated alt data is high because standard satellite and card data are commoditized.
revenue_model: Sector-index subscriptions of $30k to $150k a year, custom facility watchlists, a raw API tier, and per-project reports for private-credit lenders and site-selection teams. Drivers are paid per report, so unit economics are strongly positive.
non_obvious_insight: Truckers are the only people who physically stand in line at the real economy every day. A driver notices 'the mill's outbound lot is empty at 2pm Tuesday' or 'this DC is turning away appointments' weeks before it shows up in ISM or earnings. Telematics sells dwell minutes, but only a human sees the commodity mix, the closed dock doors and the mood in the queue, and drivers already trade this information on CB and in Facebook groups for free. This is a new data category, not an improvement to freight software.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 drivers across three freight regions (Gulf Coast, Midwest steel belt, Inland Empire) via Facebook groups and pay $5 per accepted report via instant payment. Cover 20 facilities weekly for 4 weeks. Backtest the index against public earnings and shipment data. Pitch 10 small funds through alt-data brokers and direct outreach with a free 30-day trial on 10 tickers. Charge $2k to $5k a month pilots after the trial.

title: Death Certificate Sign-Off Copilot for Hospices
one_liner: Get physicians to complete valid cause-of-death certifications in hours instead of days, sold to the hospices and care groups that get blamed for the delay, with funeral homes as the free wedge.
customer: Hospice organizations and nursing-home or assisted-living groups. The buyer is the VP of operations or hospice medical director, motivated by family-experience scores and clinician time. Funeral homes use a free version that seeds the data.
problem: Nothing moves until a physician completes the medical section of the death certificate in the state's electronic system. Cremation authorization, burial permits and certified copies for the family all wait. Doctors forget logins, delegate poorly, or enter invalid cause-of-death chains such as 'cardiac arrest', which triggers rejections or medical examiner referrals. A funeral director spends hours per case chasing certifiers, families see the delay as the funeral home's fault, and the cooler fills up while everyone waits.
solution: Phase one is a free web and text tool for funeral homes. They log each pending certificate, and the tool sends the certifier a one-tap reminder with clear instructions and shows a status page. Phase two is the paid hospice product: from the discharge summary or chart export, an AI drafts the Part I/Part II cause-of-death chain in line with NCHS conventions, flags ME-reportable triggers before submission, and routes a mobile magic-link for physician review. In states that allow certifier designees, hospice staff do the data entry. A dashboard shows time-to-certify by physician and site, with escalation rules.
why_now: Electronic death registration systems are now near-universal, so a digital workflow is possible. LLMs can reliably summarize a chart for physician review in a way that wasn't safe or cheap a few years ago. Hospice growth and public CAHPS Hospice scores raise the stakes of family experience. Medical director workloads are rising with physician shortages.
revenue_model: $35-$60 per certificate processed, or $200-$500/month per hospice site plus per-certifier seats. Optional $99/month funeral-home tier with analytics and multi-hospice benchmarking. Later, sell the anonymized time-to-certify benchmark to hospice chains and payers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone blames the funeral home for slowness, but we spend more time chasing doctors than doing the actual work. This 'post-death workflow orphan' sits after the patient leaves the EHR workflow, so no health-tech vendor sees it. The funeral home is the only party who measures days-from-death-to-certificate. So sell backwards: give funeral homes a free chase tool, collect the scorecard on which hospices and doctors are slow, then walk into those hospices with their own numbers.
first_30_days: Build the no-PHI funeral-home chase tool (case ID, certifier name and phone, state) in two weeks. Recruit 15 funeral homes in two states through the state association. After 60 days publish an anonymized 'days-to-certify by hospice' scorecard. Book meetings with the three slowest hospices and offer a $2,000/month pilot with a signed BAA. Have a physician advisor review the cause-of-death logic.

title: Model-of-Origin Forensics for AI Music Catalogs
one_liner: Attribute a track to the generator and version that made it, so catalog owners and litigators can separate legacy unlicensed-model output from the rest.
customer: Distributors, sync and production-music libraries, entertainment law firms and insurers, plus brand legal teams clearing ad music.
problem: Suno replaced its models on Sep 9 with one trained on licensed music, after label suits. A second UMG/Sony suit over roughly 60k songs is reported (single source, verify). Warner settled. Tens of millions of tracks from older models are already distributed or embedded in videos and ads. Downstream legal exposure is unproven, but risk-averse counsel will want to know which tracks came from which model. Deezer's detector answers 'AI or not,' and is licensed only to platforms.
solution: A classifier and evidence report attributing audio to a generator family and version range (Suno, Udio, Stable Audio, ElevenLabs Music and others), trained on labeled corpora we generate ourselves from paid subscriptions to each version. Output: family, version range, confidence, and whether a post-Aug 6 Suno watermark is present. Includes catalog-level exposure heat maps, a batch API, and expert-witness-ready reports.
why_now: Suno's Sep 9 model swap and Aug 6 watermarking pledge create a hard before-and-after line. Pre-watermark, pre-swap tracks are exactly the legacy tail that needs forensic attribution, and the lawsuits make the question urgent.
revenue_model: $0.05-0.25 per track for batch screening, $5-50k per catalog audit, $15-75k per litigation-grade report, and annual retainers for law firms and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'AI or not' detectors, which are crowded and sell at consumer prices ($20/month). Nobody sells 'which model, which version, before or after the licensed swap.' That is the question that maps to legal liability, so it prices like legal risk.
first_30_days: Subscribe to the major generators and produce about 5k labeled tracks per version. Get a baseline classifier working in three weeks. Approach five sync libraries and two boutique entertainment-law firms, and sell $10k pilot audits of a 20k-track catalog subset.

title: Predict Walk-In Cooler Failures Via Refrigeration Techs
one_liner: White-label predictive monitoring that local commercial-refrigeration companies sell as a maintenance plan, so a failing compressor becomes a Tuesday service visit rather than a Saturday-night emergency.
customer: Independent commercial refrigeration and HVAC-R service companies with 5-50 techs, who pay roughly $8-12 per monitored compressor per month and resell at $25-40 inside a maintenance plan. The restaurant is the end payer. A later add-on is a spoilage-insurer premium discount.
problem: A walk-in dies on Saturday at 9pm. That means an emergency call at 2-3x the rate and $8-15k of protein and dairy in the dumpster, sometimes a closed kitchen. Temperature-probe alerts only fire after the box is already warm, so they are too late. The real early signals are in the power draw: rising duty cycle from dirty condenser coils, failing fan motors and capacitors, low charge, short-cycling, and defrost heater faults. Techs spend their weekends on emergencies and have almost no recurring revenue.
solution: Clip-on current-sensing hardware (roughly $25-40 bill of materials) with a cellular or Wi-Fi gateway on each compressor and condenser fan. A model compares duty cycle and amp draw against ambient kitchen temperature and defrost cycles to flag drift weeks before the box warms. It creates a scheduled work order in the contractor's dispatch system (for example ServiceTitan) with the likely fault and parts to bring. The contractor sells it as a 'Sunday-proof plan' and gets the white-label dashboard and monthly reports.
why_now: Cellular IoT and current sensors are very cheap. Field-service software has spread through small trades, so integrations are possible. Skilled refrigeration techs are scarce and contractors need each tech to cover more boxes. The HFC phasedown (AIM Act) is changing refrigerants and service complexity, pushing repair-versus-replace decisions. Power prices are climbing, so efficiency drift now costs owners visibly.
revenue_model: Recurring B2B2B: $8-12 per monitored compressor per month to the contractor, plus hardware at cost and a per-contractor platform fee. Later, add insurer partnerships that pay for verified spoilage-loss reductions.
non_obvious_insight: The real distribution channel for restaurant equipment tech is not SaaS marketing to owners. It is 'my guy': the one refrigeration tech who answers his phone. Owners trust him, he holds the keys and the relationship, and he hates 2am calls and lacks recurring revenue. Sell to Mike, not to me. The signal is also cheaper than probes: amp draw predicts failures that temperature only reveals when it is too late.
first_30_days: Instrument 10-15 compressors and condenser fans across my two locations and five friends' restaurants with off-the-shelf clamp sensors. Log data and record every failure. Sign 2-3 local refrigeration companies as design partners with a free 60-day pilot of 50 sensors. Use the first 'caught it before Saturday' event as the case study, then sell the plan to that contractor's other accounts.

title: Peak-Load Call Service for Mid-Size Factories
one_liner: Predict the handful of hours a year that set a facility's capacity charge and alert the plant manager to cut load, paid as a share of verified savings.
customer: Commercial and industrial sites of 300 kW to 5 MW in PJM (and ERCOT 4CP) territories that demand-response aggregators ignore: cold storage, water and wastewater plants, plastics and aggregates producers, ice rinks and indoor farms. Energy brokers and consultants are the channel.
problem: A customer's capacity tag (PLC) is set by usage during a few system-peak hours, and its cost then sits on every bill for a year. PJM capacity prices have risen roughly tenfold since 2024/25, with recent auctions clearing at the cap of about $330/MW-day, so a 1 MW site's tag is worth six figures. Owners either never curtail and overpay, or curtail on 20+ hot days and lose production. Aggregators skim 20 to 40% and focus on large accounts.
solution: Model the probability that each upcoming hour ranks in the system's top peaks for the site's zone or utility rules. Use weather ensembles, load forecasts, calendar effects and, critically, the season's running maximum so far. Send a text or BMS signal with the expected value of curtailing against the plant's own curtailment cost. Cut curtailment days from about 25 to about 8 and stop alerting once the peaks have been 'caught'.
why_now: Data-center load growth has pushed PJM capacity clearing prices to the cap two auctions in a row, and those costs are now hitting commercial bills. Open AI weather ensembles (ECMWF AIFS, NOAA) make sharper probabilistic forecasts cheap. The just-finished 2026 summer is fresh evidence for a backtest pitch.
revenue_model: 20 to 25% of verified savings (measured from the next year's PLC change), a $250 to $500 monthly alert subscription, and $2K to $5K paid load audits. Brokers and consultants get a channel rebate.
non_obvious_insight: Quants see 'top 5 hours out of 4,000' as an order-statistics and optimal-stopping problem with asymmetric payoffs, not a pure forecasting problem. As the season's record load rises, the threshold to enter the top 5 becomes known, the option value of alerts collapses, and you can stop curtailing early. Incumbents earn more the more events they call, so their models over-alert. The savings show up a year later on an invoice nobody links to behavior, so customers underinvest without a counterfactual 'what your tag would have been' report.
first_30_days: Use the off-season to pull public PJM hourly load and zonal data, backtest 2019 to 2026 peaks, and generate a free 'what your tag would have been' report for 100 facilities found through EIA and utility-tariff lists. Sell $3K load audits to the first five, sign shared-savings pilots for summer 2027, and recruit two energy brokers as channel partners.

title: Savings-Group Credit Score and Treasury
one_liner: Turn informal savings groups into a credit bureau and stablecoin treasury that asset financiers can lend against.
customer: Financiers of productive assets (solar irrigation, motorbikes, milk coolers) and NGOs, with savings groups as end users.
problem: Sandi AI already reaches 10,000+ farmer groups that buy solar irrigation from pooled savings rather than loans. Chamas, VSLAs, tandas and arisan have no records that lenders can see.
solution: A WhatsApp and USSD ledger that logs contributions and minutes, produces a group credit history and optionally holds a stablecoin group treasury that diaspora members can top up. The wedge is selling qualified-group leads to asset financiers.
why_now: Kenya and Nigeria are legitimising stablecoins, local-language voice models can log minutes, and Sandi AI has shown demand.
revenue_model: $20-60 per funded asset lead, plus a 0.5% treasury fee.
non_obvious_insight: The group is the unit of trust in informal finance. Digitising it creates a bureau that cannot be scraped from mobile money data.
first_30_days: Sign 100 groups in Kenya through one NGO and record three months of contributions to prove predictive value.

title: Sleep-Apnea-to-GLP-1 Pathway for DME Suppliers
one_liner: A co-management service that lets sleep labs and CPAP suppliers prescribe, retest and retain patients as they lose weight.
customer: Independent sleep centers, home-sleep-test companies and DME suppliers whose profit engine is CPAP resupply.
problem: Zepbound was approved for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity on Dec 20, 2024, and Part D can cover it for OSA. As weight falls, patients drop CPAP without a retest or re-titration, and the DME loses resupply revenue and the patient. Sleep clinics have no pathway for prescribing or co-managing a drug.
solution: Baseline and 3/6/12-month home sleep tests, benefits verification and prior authorization for Zepbound-for-OSA, a nutrition and muscle plan, auto-CPAP pressure re-titration from device data, and a 'retest before you quit CPAP' protocol. DMEs keep the supply relationship where still needed.
why_now: The OSA indication now has Medicare and commercial coverage routes, and cash pricing is falling, so patient demand is arriving at sleep clinics without a pathway. DMEs see the threat and hold the patient data (CPAP usage) needed to co-manage.
revenue_model: $15-30 per patient per month to the DME or sleep center, or a share of retained resupply, plus per-test fees.
non_obvious_insight: The DME supplier looks like the loser but is the natural gatekeeper: it has adherence data, patient trust and a recurring billing relationship, and it will pay to convert lost resupply into a managed weight-and-airway program.
first_30_days: Approach 5 regional DMEs or sleep centers. Pilot on 100 CPAP patients with BMI of 30 or more and AHI of 15 or more. Measure PA success, retest rate and retained resupply.

title: Package Travel Surcharge Compliance for Tour Operators
one_liner: A rules engine that calculates lawful fuel-driven price increases on already-sold package tours, generates the notices and tracks the 8% cancellation trigger.
customer: Small and mid-size EU and UK package organisers, coach-tour and cruise-package sellers, and agents acting as organisers with EUR 5-200M in sales, plus their bonding insurers.
problem: With the Hormuz closure and soaring jet fuel, packages sold months ago are underwater and airlines are cutting capacity and raising fares. Under EU and UK package rules an organiser can raise prices only if the contract allows it, only for fuel, tax or exchange-rate changes, with at least 20 days' notice, and an increase above 8% lets travellers cancel free. Organisers must also pass on decreases. Spreadsheet errors mean refunds and regulator complaints.
solution: Connect to booking exports, model the cost components per trip, compute the lawful pass-through per contract clause, and generate localised notices with timelines. Track the 8% threshold and deadlines, keep an audit trail for regulators and bonding insurers, and flag contracts whose clauses need rewriting.
why_now: Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed on 2 Mar 2026 and, by September, budget carriers cite soaring fuel costs with capacity cuts and fare hikes ahead. Shorter booking lead times (33 days versus 37.5) do not help packages sold long in advance.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per operator or about 0.1% of sales, plus per-notice fees and clause redesign consulting.
non_obvious_insight: In a cost shock much of the loss is legal rather than commercial. Operators eat costs because they misread pass-through limits or send defective notices, so compliance software turns panic into recovered margin.
first_30_days: Build a calculator and notice templates in a spreadsheet plus an LLM. Publish a gated '2026 fuel surcharge playbook' through trade associations, and sell 10 operators at EUR 500 per month.

title: Ratepayer Impact Statements for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, quantified 'who pays' filing for every proposed data center, like an environmental impact statement but for your electric bill.
customer: Data center developers who need a credible neutral document to win zoning or PUC approval ($50-150k per project). County governments, state consumer advocates and ratepayer coalitions ($15-40k per docket) also buy it.
problem: 7 in 10 Americans oppose data centers in their community and New York imposed a hyperscale moratorium. Residential rates are up 7.3% and utilities requested a record $31B in hikes in 2025. Nobody can credibly say how much of a specific rate case or interconnection cost a given project causes, so each side hires ad hoc experts and the fight runs on vibes.
solution: An open, auditable cost-causation model built on FERC Form 1, EIA-861, large-load tariff filings, IRP capacity plans and PJM auction results. It outputs a 10-year per-household bill delta for a specific project under different tariff terms (minimum take, collateral, bring-your-own-capacity). Deliverables are a standardized Ratepayer Impact Statement and a witness-ready exhibit. A free state-by-state 'who pays' scorecard is the top of the funnel.
why_now: Affordability is a midterm issue and opposition is now bill-driven. Utilities are adopting large-load tariffs whose terms can be modeled. Capacity prices at the cap make cost shifts visible in dollars per MWh.
revenue_model: Per-project fee from developers, per-docket fee from advocates and counties, and an annual subscription for PUC staff. Independence comes from a published fee schedule and a methodology committed in advance, as with credit rating agencies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders dismiss opposition as NIMBY, but it is really about bills, and bills are quantifiable. Whoever owns the accepted number owns the approval process. Both sides will pay for it, the way both sides accept an appraisal.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Who Pays' report for three states using public filings. Email 10 state consumer advocate offices and 20 county planning departments. Offer a $12k pilot impact statement on one live docket. Approach two mid-size developers who are stuck in a zoning fight.

title: Vacant Inherited-Home Insurance and Caretaking
one_liner: A bundled insurance-plus-sensors-plus-caretaker program for the house that sits empty during probate.
customer: Executors and heirs of a decedent's home, reached through probate attorneys, funeral homes and hospice social workers. Insurers and MGAs are the capacity partners.
problem: Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage for vandalism, freezing and other perils once a home is vacant 30-60 days, which is exactly when no probate court has appointed anyone. Probate often takes 9-18 months (unverified estimate). A burst pipe or break-in lands on an amateur executor, who may be personally exposed. Property taxes and utilities also keep running.
solution: An MGA-backed 'Estate Home Program' with a vacant-dwelling policy placed with a surplus-lines carrier, water and temperature sensors, weekly visits, lock rekeying and mail handling, utility transfer to the executor, and an optional executor advance for carrying costs repaid at sale. Add clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
why_now: Housing wealth is starting to flow from Boomers. Insurers tightened property underwriting after recent nonrenewal waves, and cheap IoT sensors make monitoring practical.
revenue_model: MGA commission (10-20%), a $150-$300/month program fee, and margin on clean-out and sale-prep referrals.
non_obvious_insight: The house effectively becomes uninsurable at the exact moment the owner dies, and nobody owns that timing gap. Executors find out after the loss.
first_30_days: Find an E&S broker who writes vacant dwellings and design a 'vacant estate' placement. Sign 5 probate attorneys and test with 10 houses. Confirm state vacancy and insurable-interest rules with a licensed agent.

title: Rural Jail Pharmacy-in-a-Box for Independents
one_liner: Turn the local independent's blister packing, delivery and controlled-substance discipline into a per-inmate contract for the county jail that the sheriff is afraid of.
customer: Sheriffs, jail administrators and county commissions running jails of about 20-150 beds, whose risk pools and insurers care about medication liability. Independent pharmacies are a second customer, licensing the playbook and software.
problem: Jail medication is a sheriff's biggest lawsuit exposure: missed doses, withdrawal, wrong-inmate errors, controlled-substance counts. Small jails run it with a deputy, a clipboard and a nurse who visits two days a week. Mail-order jail pharmacies take 3-5 days, so first-night meds come from the ER or a deputy's personal trip to the drugstore. Buprenorphine and other opioid-treatment mandates funded by opioid settlements add complexity. Meanwhile local independents already run the identical workflow for nursing homes.
solution: A repeatable program with same-day intake verification (call the outside pharmacy, check the PDMP). Barcode blister-packed med pass with an offline-capable eMAR on a tablet. Controlled-substance counts with dual sign-off and photo audit. An emergency kit and a monthly consultant-pharmacist review. A 30-day bridge supply at release. Sold as a playbook, software and group-purchasing bundle so any independent can become the county's jail pharmacy, with master agreements through state association-of-counties risk pools.
why_now: Wellpath's late-2024 bankruptcy and the contract turnover that followed left counties scrambling for medical vendors. Deaths-in-custody litigation keeps rising. Opioid-settlement dollars are flowing to county jails for medication for opioid use disorder. A growing number of state Medicaid reentry waivers require medication continuity at release. Independents need any revenue line that does not depend on PBM reimbursement.
revenue_model: County per-diem or monthly retainer (roughly $1,500-6,000 a month per small jail, to be validated by state). The pharmacy pays a 10-15% platform fee plus $300-600 a month for the software. Additional revenue from risk-pool partnership programs and discharge-supply services.
non_obvious_insight: Rural jail medication is not a healthcare problem, it is a liability problem the sheriff cannot outsource to a national vendor that ships in five days. The real buyer is the county risk pool and insurer, and the independent pharmacist next door is the only entity that can deliver in thirty minutes. Small contracts often fall below county bid thresholds, and the sheriff already knows the pharmacist by first name.
first_30_days: The pharmacist calls the sheriff in their own county and offers a 60-day pilot at cost. Audit the jail's med room and write a one-page deficiency list. Propose eMAR plus packaging. Check the state pharmacy board's rules for institutional or correctional pharmacy licensure. Pitch the results to the state sheriffs' association and the county risk pool, and recruit two neighboring independents to copy the model.

title: Own-Your-Office Buyer Groups for Practices
one_liner: Assemble dentists, clinics, law and accounting firms into buyer clubs that buy discounted vacant office buildings and split them into owner-occupied condos financed with SBA loans.
customer: Small professional practices renting 3,000-15,000 sf each (5-20 per building), plus special servicers and receivers who need a bulk exit for distressed office.
problem: National office vacancy is 17.8%, office CMBS delinquency 13.2%, $39B of office debt matures within 12 months and $289B by 2028 on about 14,000 properties. Sellers are forced, but institutional buyers price office as an income asset and few small buyers can act. Small practices keep paying roughly $33 asking rent with escalators and never see the building trade at a fraction of replacement cost.
solution: Pre-qualify 8-15 owner-users (financials and SBA 504/7(a) eligibility), find 40-150k sf Class B buildings from servicers at low per-sf bases, create a condo declaration and a single purchasing entity, close in bulk, then finance and deed units individually to practices (each occupying its own space). Keep the association-management and repositioning contract.
why_now: Servicers are actively seeking exits and most B/C buildings do not pencil for residential conversion, so owner-occupancy is the highest and best use. SBA programs finance owner-occupants at very high LTV, and high rates make a lease a large fixed cost relative to ownership.
revenue_model: 2-4% sponsor fee per unit sold, condo-ization margin or promote on unsold units, and recurring building/association management ($0.60-1.00 per sf per year) plus resale commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Investors value office on cash-flow multiples, while owner-users value it at the rent they would otherwise pay. At distressed bases the owner-user's willingness to pay can exceed the investor's bid, and no one is aggregating this fragmented demand against a forced-seller supply pool.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with cheap Class B office. Launch a landing page and outreach through dental, medical and CPA associations and SBA/CDC lenders. Collect 10 non-binding letters of intent from practices. Approach 2-3 servicer asset managers about bulk-sale listings. Charge a refundable $2,500 deposit for founding-member slots.

title: Federal-Equipment Disposition Desk for Closing Labs
one_liner: A compliance-plus-resale service that clears federal-interest, decontaminates and re-homes grant-funded instruments when labs shrink or close.
customer: University research-administration and property offices, independent research institutes, SBIR-funded startups winding down, and the roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs Owl Posting counts.
problem: Instruments bought with federal funds carry federal-interest and disposition rules (2 CFR 200.313, with a per-unit threshold), which stall resale. Freezers, cryostats and sequencers sit idle or get trashed. NIH grant terminations, 15,000+ biopharma job cuts and 50+ shrinking companies add supply, while small labs cannot afford new equipment. The brief flags used-equipment liquidation for squeezed labs as an underserved gap.
solution: An asset-level 'federal-interest passport': identify the award and agency, determine the obligation, prepare disposition requests and valuation, arrange decontamination certificates, pack and ship, and list to vetted buyers. Commission plus compliance fee.
why_now: Funding turbulence and layoffs are producing lab closures now, and marketplaces for used equipment exist but do not solve permission or liability.
revenue_model: 15-25% commission on resale, $500-2,500 per-asset compliance fees, and institutional annual retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The seller's pain is permission and liability, not price discovery, so marketplaces do not fix it. The compliance passport is the unlock, and attaching one at purchase time makes instruments 'resale-ready' and turns the desk into a recurring service.
first_30_days: Contact 10 mid-tier university property or research-admin offices and 30 winding-down SBIR startups. Process 5 pilot disposals. Template the passport. Partner with a decontamination and shipping vendor.

title: The Junior Bench: Rent-a-Resident for AI Review
one_liner: Mid-size accounting, legal and insurance firms rent trained new grads for 12 weeks to verify their AI-produced work, rebuilding the vanished junior rung as a paid residency.
customer: Regional accounting firms, boutique law firms, insurance brokerages and healthcare revenue-cycle companies; new grads join as paid residents.
problem: Employers stopped hiring juniors because AI does the grunt work, yet they still need future seniors. AI-exposed majors have 5 points lower initial employment, grads are 42% underemployed, and 22-25 year-olds in exposed jobs are 19% below trend. Meanwhile firms carry liability for AI-drafted work that nobody is trained to verify well.
solution: A cohort residency. Two weeks of domain and AI-verification training, then about ten weeks embedded in the firm's workflow reviewing AI-drafted workpapers, contract abstracts or claims against sources, with seeded-error scoring. The firm pays a weekly rate and can convert residents to hires. Each resident builds a scored 'verification record' that becomes the credential.
why_now: Payroll data show a widening hiring gap since August 2025. Firms are AI-first but facing quality and liability incidents, and partner pipelines will look empty in about five years.
revenue_model: About $1,800-2,500 per resident-week from the firm against roughly $900-1,100 wage cost, giving 40-50% gross margin. Optional conversion fee if hired early.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not remove the junior job; it turned it from doing into checking. Checking is a trainable, measurable skill with an obvious buyer: the firm that carries the liability for AI errors.
first_30_days: Sell to 3 regional CPA firms ahead of busy season with 5 residents each. Recruit from local accounting grads. Build an error-injection test set to score residents. Charge from week one.

title: Last Day Co: Small Business Wind-Down
one_liner: A flat-fee retirement service for owners who do not want to sell, just stop: legal wind-down, lease exit, records custody, customer-list handoff and a proper last day.
customer: Retiring owners of solo and micro businesses with $100k to $2M in revenue. Start with regulated solo practices (therapists, small medical or dental practices, solo attorneys, CPAs) where closing duties create urgency, then salons, restaurants and contractors.
problem: McKinsey estimates baby boomers run as many as 6M small and midsize US businesses, with roughly 2.3M to 3M expected to transition ownership this decade, yet only about 54% of owners have a succession plan and about a third of owners over 50 say they cannot find a buyer. Brokers are paid only on sales and skip tiny firms, so most simply shut. That leaves leases, personal guarantees, client records, final payroll and taxes, licenses and customers stranded.
solution: A productized 90-day closure: state and local filings and final taxes through a partner CPA, lease exit negotiation (buyout or assignment, limiting the personal guarantee), equipment and inventory liquidation, and a records-custody service where Last Day Co acts as professional custodian for 7 to 10 years with client notice and a release process. It also brokers the customer list or goodwill to a vetted local competitor, with a fee to the owner. It closes with a last-day package: customer letter, farewell event, staff reference packets.
why_now: Boomers are now roughly 62 to 80, so closures are rising toward the McKinsey-projected peak. LLMs make state-specific closure checklists, notices and letters cheap to produce accurately. Remote records custody removes the need for a physical archive.
revenue_model: A $2,500 to $9,000 flat wind-down fee. Records custody at $25 to $75 per month or a prepaid $1,500 for 7 years. A goodwill-handoff success fee of 10% to 20% of what the acquirer pays. A 10% to 15% liquidation commission.
non_obvious_insight: Brokers sell, and nobody closes. Most owners do not want a sale process, they want to stop, so the real product is permission and completion with liability handled. Custodianship for regulated practices is near-zero-churn recurring revenue, and the customer list is the only asset that survives a closure, so a warm handoff to a neighboring competitor is where the money is.
first_30_days: Pick solo therapists and solo attorneys in one state. With a local attorney and CPA, write the state-specific 'professional will and closure' playbook. Sell the $299 professional will plus closure plan through the state association newsletter and LinkedIn. Do three discounted pilot closures end to end, build a list of local acquirers for goodwill handoffs, and document each step as a repeatable checklist.

title: Voice-Agent Cash-Price Negotiator for Imaging
one_liner: AI voice agents that call 20-30 local facilities, negotiate a guaranteed cash bundle for an MRI, CT or scope, and book it for the newly uninsured.
customer: Uninsured and high-deductible patients (Urban estimates 4.8M newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry; subsidy-cliff self-employed), small employers, and imaging centers, labs and ASCs with idle capacity.
problem: Posted prices are inconsistent and unusable, and cash prices for the same MRI can differ ~10x. Patients will not make 20 phone calls or negotiate, while facilities have idle slots.
solution: The patient submits an order. Agents call and email facilities for real quotes and slot availability, negotiate global-fee prepay bundles, filter for accreditation and quality, return one guaranteed price and book, with escrowed payment.
why_now: Real-time voice agents became reliable in 2025-26, and coverage loss is growing (ACA subsidies expired; Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027). Posted-price marketplaces exist but they don't negotiate dynamically.
revenue_model: $19-39 per booked procedure plus a 5-10% fee from facilities filling otherwise idle slots (cash-pay only, structured to avoid federal-program referral issues).
non_obvious_insight: Cash price is a negotiated market for empty slots. Discovery cost used to be too high per patient, and voice agents make it nearly free.
first_30_days: Concierge 50 MRI, CT and colonoscopy quotes in one metro with call scripts and an LLM voice agent on top. Publish the price spread, sign 5 imaging centers, and charge $29 per booking.

title: Offline Brain for Talking Toys
one_liner: A sub-$20 on-device speech-and-language module that lets toys hold child-safe conversations with no cloud, no audio leaving the toy and parent-readable summaries on the parent's phone.
customer: Toy brands and ODMs, indie AI-toy startups and kids' IP licensors who fear cloud data liability.
problem: Cloud-based AI toys stream children's voices to servers, which the amended COPPA rule (biometrics, retention limits, separate opt-in for third-party sharing) makes risky. Brand exposure is rising after consumer tests and lawsuits. Toy makers lack model-safety teams, and per-conversation cloud costs collide with a one-time hardware sale.
solution: A reference design and software stack: kid-tuned speech recognition, a 1-4B-parameter model fine-tuned for age-banded personas and refusals, and text-to-speech on a $10-15 NPU chip. Safety-locked story and play modes, and Bluetooth summaries to a parent app. Licensed to ODMs, with dev kits for startups.
why_now: Small on-device models reached conversational quality in 2025-26 and cheap NPUs run them in real time, so the technology only just became feasible. Regulation turns cloud audio into a liability, and holiday 2026 is the first big AI-toy season.
revenue_model: $2-4 per unit licence, $299 dev kits, and paid NRE for custom personas.
non_obvious_insight: The cloud is both the risk and the cost. On-device removes marginal cost and turns COPPA from a burden into a marketing claim ('nothing leaves the toy'), fixing the broken subscription-for-hardware model.
first_30_days: Prototype on a Raspberry Pi 5 or RK3588 board with an off-the-shelf small model. Measure latency and accuracy on consented child speech. Demo to 15 indie toy makers on Kickstarter and Crowd Supply and to 2 ODMs. Aim for 2 paid dev-kit pilots with $5k NRE each.

title: Vet-Supervised Cattle Crews for the Screwworm Era
one_liner: Custom-harvester-style crews do the 80% of a vet's working day that is labor (inspect, treat navels, tag, record) so the scarce vet supervises and signs instead of holding the chute.
customer: Ranchers in screwworm zones and buffer states (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma) paying per head or per day; sale barns, stocker operations and feedlots that need pre-movement inspection documentation; and overloaded rural vet practices that subcontract overflow to a crew.
problem: Only about 1.3% of vets work in food animal practice, and South Texas vets say it will not be physically possible to handle every screwworm case. Daily inspection is the core control, newborn calves' navels are prime targets (past outbreaks saw navel strike rates as high as 50% in unprotected calves), and ranchers with 300-3,000 head across brush country do not have the labor to look at every animal every day.
solution: A vet-supervised service company (a rural vet as medical director, or a vet-owned entity) fielding 3-4 person crews with a trailer: portable squeeze chute, EID reader, wound-care kit, vet-approved treatment protocols, and a photo- and GPS-stamped inspection log that the vet countersigns. The seasonal product is an 'NWS Season Program' of scheduled pasture rounds, navel treatment on newborn calves, wound checks, prescribed prophylactic treatments under an existing VCPR, and movement paperwork. Off-season the same crews run preg-checks, weaning, vaccination and processing days year-round, with the vet doing exams and sign-off.
why_now: The first US screwworm detections came in Texas in June 2026, followed by more counties, a New Mexico detection, and the first infested horse in September. Sterile fly supply is constrained, federal and state agencies have imposed movement restrictions and mandatory veterinary inspections in affected areas, and FDA has moved to authorize treatment products. Spring calving in Texas is the next high-risk window.
revenue_model: $3-8 per head per treatment or round, day rates around $1,800-2,500 per crew for working days, seasonal retainer contracts, and a 20-30% margin on subcontracted overflow from vet practices. Target roughly 35-40% gross margin per crew.
non_obvious_insight: The vet shortage is largely a labor-allocation problem: a $250-per-hour license is spent on tasks that only need hands. Custom crews are normal for harvest, hay and branding, but herd health stayed in-house because vets never delegated it formally. Practice-of-veterinary-medicine laws let a supervising vet delegate many tasks, and once the vet is medical director of record the boundary is workable. The durable asset is the trained crew that keeps earning long after screwworm fades, because labor-short ranches will keep buying it.
first_30_days: Sign 2 overloaded vets in Texas or New Mexico as medical directors, and confirm what each state's practice act allows non-vets to do. Buy a used portable chute, trailer and 2 EID readers (about $15K), recruit 3 experienced ranch hands or vet-tech students, and get liability coverage. Sell 5 ranches a fall program of weaning-time inspections and navel and wound checks on fall-calving herds, then sell the spring calving program from the results.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

title: After-Death Home Reset for Hospice Families
one_liner: A two-person crew that returns the house to normal within 48 hours of a home hospice death: bed out, meds destroyed, room restored, memory box packed.
customer: Hospice agencies pay per home death, as a family-experience and bereavement differentiator. A second stream is families paying a premium, and funeral homes reselling it as an add-on.
problem: After a home death the hospital bed, oxygen concentrator and commode often sit in the living room for days. The DME vendor schedules pickup on its own clock. The leftover morphine, lorazepam and haloperidol 'comfort kit' sits in the fridge or cabinet. Nurses are supposed to see to disposal, but the home visit is often skipped or rushed, and families quietly keep or mis-dispose of them. The dead person's glasses, dentures and hearing aids end up in a drawer. The family remembers the empty bed in the middle of the room for the rest of their lives. The CAHPS Hospice family survey arrives months later and those last impressions color the answers.
solution: A chaplain-designed protocol delivered by two trained, background-checked staff in a branded van. On admission, the hospice photographs the room so the crew can restore the original furniture layout. Within 24 to 48 hours of death the crew coordinates or performs bed and equipment removal, destroys leftover controlled drugs with deactivation pouches and a witnessed log the hospice can put in the chart, and launders linens. They pack a memory box (glasses, jewelry, a worn shirt, the last handwritten note). They restore the room, open the windows, and offer a two-minute optional blessing or silence. A hand-off card tells the family what happens at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
why_now: Hospice is consolidating, with private equity and large chains competing on public CAHPS-based quality scores that drive referrals. Regulators and communities are paying more attention to opioid diversion. Hospice per-diem margins are squeezed and the DME vendors they use are getting slower and cheaper. Home is where most hospice deaths occur. Also, nurses are stretched thin, so the care they used to give informally in that first day is disappearing, and nobody owns it.
revenue_model: Hospice pays $250 to $400 per home death on a per-case contract, with volume tiers. Families or funeral homes pay $450 to $600 for a premium version with a full room refresh and donation pickup for clothing and mobility aids. A hospice with roughly 100 patients on service has on the order of 25 to 35 deaths a month, around half at home, so three hospices support a small crew. Sponsorship from a nonprofit hospice foundation can cover indigent families.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the crisis is the moment of death. Insiders know the emotional injury persists in the physical room and in the loose ends nobody owns: the bed, the drugs, the dentures. The hospice would love to solve it but cannot bill for it and the nurse has already left. Whoever owns hours 6 through 48 after death, when the funeral home has taken the body and all clinical staff have gone, owns the family's memory of the hospice.
first_30_days: Sign one small nonprofit hospice as a design partner. Write the checklist with the chaplain, the DON and a pharmacist for the controlled-drug disposal log. Buy a used van, get general liability coverage, and hire two people with home-health-aide or hospitality backgrounds. Do the first 5 to 8 resets free in exchange for family feedback. Charge from case 9, and ask the hospice's quality director to compare family feedback scores with and without the reset.

title: Battery-Free Soil Tags Read by Drone
one_liner: Disposable soil moisture and salinity tags that need no battery and are read by drone flyover.
customer: Agronomy service providers, co-ops and specialty-crop growers with irrigated fields.
problem: Farmers face fertilizer and diesel volatility with no pricing power, yet soil data stays sparse because sensors cost too much and need batteries.
solution: Sub-$3 ambient-backscatter tags placed at planting and read from a drone or planter-mounted reader, starting with moisture and salinity and adding nitrate later.
why_now: Ambient-IoT chips scaled in 2025, and urea swinging from $400 to $850 to about $453/t makes precise input use valuable.
revenue_model: Per-tag fee plus a per-acre mapping and reading service.
non_obvious_insight: Soil sampling stays sparse because sensors are expensive. Making them disposable makes dense maps feasible.
first_30_days: Buy ambient-IoT development kits, prove drone readout at short range, and run a small field pilot on two farms.

title: Boundary Truth: Ledger of Special-District Lines
one_liner: Turn recorded annexation, inclusion and exclusion instruments into a single authoritative boundary ledger that catches wrong tax bills, wrong ballots and wrong 911 routing.
customer: County assessors and treasurers, election offices, state 911 boards and NG911 GIS coordinators, plus special-district management firms and metro-district law firms. Paid through the recorder's technology or preservation fund (spendable at the recorder's discretion in many states), election grant money or 911 fee funds.
problem: There are about 39,000 special districts (fire, water, library, mosquito, metro) and their boundary changes are recorded with the county clerk as ministerial filings with no downstream notification. Nobody reliably updates the assessor's tax-area codes, the election office's address-to-district crosswalk or the 911 emergency-service boundary layer. Result: parcels billed by the wrong district or by none (lost revenue, later refunds), voters handed the wrong ballot style, and dispatch mismatches. State attorneys general have issued opinions on tax levies made after officials weren't notified of boundary changes. We discover the errors in the last two weeks before an election or when a taxpayer complains.
solution: An AI pipeline reads the recorded instruments (metes-and-bounds text, plats, ordinances), draws polygons with closure and area sanity checks, and routes low-confidence ones to a human reviewer. It keeps a versioned, effective-dated ledger of each district's legal boundary. It then diffs the ledger against the assessor's tax-area file, the voter address crosswalk and the 911 boundary layer, and returns a plain exception list such as '312 parcels inside Fire District 4 per the 2022 recorded inclusion but billed to no district.' Sell a fixed-price audit first, then an annual subscription.
why_now: Mid-decade redistricting fights and the 2026 midterms have made ballot-style accuracy politically radioactive. NG911 requires clean authoritative boundary GIS data. Property tax scrutiny makes every misbilled dollar a headline. LLMs can now parse legal descriptions well enough to draft polygons that a human reviews rather than draws.
revenue_model: $15k-$40k one-time boundary drift audit per county, then $10k-$30k/year per county for continuous monitoring, sized to fit inside a recorder's technology fund or a 911 board budget. Data-quality add-ons for district management firms and bond counsel.
non_obvious_insight: The legal boundary is the recorded instrument, not the GIS layer; the layer is just someone's drawing of a PDF. Because the clerk often sits at the junction of records, elections and sometimes tax, we see the stale cascade that assessors, election staff and 911 GIS analysts each see only a slice of. Also, the clerk's tech fund often sits outside the commissioners' budget fight, so a $25k audit can be approved in weeks, not the 18 months that scares govtech investors.
first_30_days: Pick one state heavy on special districts (Colorado metro districts, Texas MUDs and ESDs, Illinois, Washington, Florida CDDs). Offer a free boundary drift audit to a single county's assessor and clerk using five years of recorded inclusions and annexations. Turn the mismatch list into a paid pilot funded from the recorder's fund, then take the proof to the state 911 board.

title: Solar Monitoring Data as Appliance Stethoscope
one_liner: Use the consumption data already sitting in installers' monitoring portals to spot dying air conditioners, resistance heat, hidden EVs and always-on pool pumps, then sell verified leads to HVAC and electrical contractors with a share back to the installer.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger electricians and pool contractors pay per verified lead ($100-300). Installers earn a 20-30% revenue share. A later payer could be home-warranty companies and insurers who want early-failure signals.
problem: Post-2025, residential solar installers are short of revenue and sit on 500-5,000 past customers with monitoring already attached. HVAC contractors pay $150-500 per lead and spend most of their marketing budget in peak summer emergencies. Nobody mines the consumption stream (Enphase, SolarEdge and Tesla gateways record it every 5-15 minutes), where a failing compressor, a home heated by resistance strips or a new EV shows up clearly.
solution: Install-side product called Home Energy Plus. The installer emails past customers an opt-in for a free annual system checkup, connecting to their monitoring account through the OEM's API. An anomaly model flags: an AC drawing 25%+ more than on comparable weather days, short cycling, high winter baseline (resistance heat), overnight EV signature, pool pump running 24 hours. The customer gets a plain-language report ('your AC is likely low on refrigerant; a $99 tune-up now avoids a July failure'). Contractors bid for the lead in their service area, and the installer is paid a share. Homeowners can opt out at any time.
why_now: Federal 25C and 25D credits ended Dec 31, 2025, so heat-pump and HVAC contractors need intent-rich leads. Installers need recurring revenue from existing customers as new-install volume falls in 2026. OEM monitoring APIs are open to owner-authorized apps, and anomaly-detection models are cheap. Spring and fall shoulder seasons are when contractors most want planned replacements.
revenue_model: $100-300 per lead depending on trade and job size, split 70/30 with the installer. Optional $5-10 a month homeowner subscription for continuing reports. Later, sell early-failure signals to home-warranty companies at a per-home annual fee.
non_obvious_insight: An installer's monitoring portal is a stethoscope for the whole house, but installers use it only to answer why production is low. The consumption side is unlabeled and unused. Also, homeowners already trust the installer, and consent to share data is easiest to get from that relationship. A planned replacement in shoulder season is worth more to an HVAC company than an emergency job in July, because it fills idle crews.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers with 1,000+ customers on Enphase or SolarEdge. Send the opt-in as a free annual checkup. Analyze 300 homes' historical data by hand and code up the first two signatures (AC and resistance heat). Produce 30 personalized reports. Sell the first 10 leads to two HVAC contractors at $150 each and measure close rate. Draft the consent and data-use terms with a privacy lawyer.

title: Through-the-Package Drug Verification Library
one_liner: A subscription spectral fingerprint library and scan-on-receipt workflow that lets pharmacies and wholesalers verify what is actually in a sealed vial or blister pack, using off-the-shelf handheld Raman/NIR devices.
customer: 503A/503B compounding pharmacies and telehealth GLP-1 dispensers receiving vials or API from overseas, secondary wholesalers and repackagers, hospital pharmacies, and med-spa distributors.
problem: ARPA-H states that drug-related morbidity and mortality cost $528 billion per year, that recalls affect the medication of over 150 million Americans each year, that 'most recalls only happen after patients are exposed', and that only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports, a process that takes weeks. Serialization under DSCSA tracks the box (package-level identifiers, 24-hour notification of illegitimate product), not the molecule inside it, so a convincing counterfeit or diluted vial passes every paperwork check.
solution: Do not build hardware. Rent or resell existing handheld Raman/NIR units, and build the proprietary part: a reference library of authentic and adulterated finished-dose spectra measured through blisters, vials and prefilled pens, plus a classifier and a chain-of-custody report (photo, lot number, spectrum, pass/fail/uncertain). Uncertain results route to a partner lab for confirmatory HPLC. The library improves with every scan.
why_now: ARPA-H's FASTPASS program (solicitation ARPA-H-SOL-26-160; solution summaries due September 21, 2026, full proposals November 10, 2026) is funding through-packaging sensing (TA1 SAMPLE) and analytics (TA2 DETECT), which signals that the sensing hardware and spectroscopy science are mature enough to commercialize. GLP-1 volume and compounding have widened the exposure of small dispensers who have no way to check incoming product.
revenue_model: $1 to $3 per scan (usage SaaS), $300 per month device rental, $150 to $400 per escalated lab confirmation, and $6k to $24k per year library license for wholesalers.
non_obvious_insight: DSCSA verifies labels and traceability, not contents, and ARPA-H itself says the gap is one 'no single agency, manufacturer, or current technology can close alone'. That leaves room for a private data product. The moat is the library of through-package spectra, not the scanner, and it compounds with every customer scan. Evidence: https://arpa-h.gov/explore-funding/programs/fastpass ($528B, 150M Americans, 'only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports', TA1 SAMPLE and TA2 DETECT) and https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-supply-chain-integrity/drug-supply-chain-security-act-dscsa (package-level identification and 24-hour illegitimate-product notification). Caveat: the ARPA-H page did not give product types or counterfeit prevalence, and the GLP-1 exposure is my inference from public FDA alerts.
first_30_days: Pick 10 high-volume SKUs (injectable GLP-1 vials and pens plus a few high-value generics). Buy authentic references, make in-house dilution and wrong-API samples with a partner lab, rent two handhelds, and collect spectra through the packaging. Offer 3 compounding pharmacies and 2 regional wholesalers a free 30-day pilot with scan-on-receipt. Convert to paid on a per-scan plan. Skip the FASTPASS proposal unless a university partner handles it.

title: Care-First Reverse Mortgages With Locked Payouts
one_liner: A care-planning broker that funds long-term care from home equity and releases the money only to verified caregivers and facilities.
customer: Homeowners 70-85 with $300k+ equity and thin liquid savings, or their adult children holding a power of attorney. The channel is elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers and hospital discharge planners.
problem: Long-term-care insurance is failing policyholders: Genworth has about $31.8B of approved premium hikes, and 2023 hikes averaged 51%. Care runs $75-115k a year, and Medicaid retrenchment is coming. The one big asset is home equity, but advisors still treat reverse mortgages as a last resort and lump sums invite fraud and sibling fights.
solution: Start with a 12-month care budget and plan. Match it to a reverse-mortgage line of credit (HECM or proprietary), through an NMLS-licensed broker or a co-brokering partner. Then open a care wallet: funds go only to vetted payees (agency, facility, or a family caregiver under a documented personal-care agreement with payroll), with a ledger for siblings and Medicaid look-back records, and multi-party approval for any other outflow.
why_now: Proprietary reverse mortgages now hold 52% share against 48% for HECM, so products are better. Seniors hold $14.92T in home equity. LTC insurance is unravelling, the 80+ cohort is exploding, and elder fraud hit $7.7B in 2025 (up 59%), which makes lump-sum liquidity risky without controls.
revenue_model: Broker origination compensation on funded loans, roughly 1-2% of loan amount, plus a $49 a month care-wallet fee. Licensing the wallet to lenders as a fraud-protection differentiator is later upside.
non_obvious_insight: The product isn't the loan; it's controlled disbursement plus a care plan. Reverse mortgages are viewed with suspicion because of how the cash gets spent, and a locked, audited payout stream fixes the exact failure mode that ruined the category's reputation.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed reverse-mortgage broker, publish 'how to pay for care with home equity' content, and build referral relationships with 10 elder-law firms and care managers. Loans close in about 60-75 days, so first revenue lands inside six months.
